entries.title: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large exchange of prisoners of war, officials say
entries.summary: Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war. U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi led to this decision, marking the biggest humanitarian release since the war began in 2022.
entries.content:
Russia and Ukraine agree to a large exchange of prisoners of war, officials say

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Officials at U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine said Wednesday that the sides have agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, said after the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended.

Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv's delegation in Abu Dhabi, confirmed the planned exchange.

Hopes were low for any major breakthrough in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped prisoners during their nearly five-year war.

U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.

Kushner says he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration has to reckon with Democrats, who could demand more support for Ukraine, taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections.

Also, Russia's wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.

Umerov said Kyiv's delegation is expected to meet Wednesday with European officials.

Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. However, representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and were consulting with the Ukrainian delegation, officials said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday's session was "constructive and quite substantive."

The talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including possible prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country, he said.

Security guarantees also were discussed, he said. However, Russia and Ukraine have shown no sign of a willingness to compromise on their demands.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting "very productive," while cautioning that a breakthrough on stopping the war will take time.

The Abu Dhabi talks are being held against the backdrop of continued fighting on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year.

Meanwhile, both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones.

Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property.

Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to the regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko.

He said that the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers.

entries.title: House effectively ends Hegseth impeachment. And, 3 men accused of plotting U.K. attacks
entries.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has been spared from the House's impeachment effort, at least for now. And, federal prosecutors arrested three men accused of being Iran-backed operatives.
entries.content:
Hegseth Impeachment Blocked, House Leadership Change, DOJ Charges Terror Suspects

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The House has effectively killed Republican Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The chamber voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment articles back to the House Judiciary Committee for review. The move circumvents any potential floor vote on the impeachment and virtually ensures it won't be addressed before the current Congress session ends. Massie had reintroduced the impeachment articles on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes related to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes against drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.

  • 🎧 NPR's Eric McDaniel describes yesterday's vote to Up First as a game of attendance. There were enough Democrats in Washington to pass the impeachment resolution, but not enough were on the floor to vote, so Republicans had the simple majority. McDaniel spoke to Warren Davidson, a GOP congressman from Ohio, the day before the vote. Davidson said he thinks the war in Iran is unconstitutional, but argued that Hegseth was just a scapegoat for the "status quo politics in Washington."
  • ➡️ The GOP had a lot on their agenda yesterday. The Republican-controlled House Oversight Committee released a report on its investigation into the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associates. The report concluded that the federal government mishandled criminal investigations into the disgraced financier and failed survivors.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio will be the new minority leader of the House. House Republicans voted yesterday to replace Speaker Mike Johnson, who is stepping down after last week's midterm losses. At 62, Jordan brings experience from the House Oversight and Judiciary committees. The two panels are poised to play a central role in the new Congress as Democrats plan investigations into President Trump and his administration.

  • 🎧 NPR's Barbara Sprunt says she viewed the election as a choice between continuity and change, and Jordan clearly represented change. Jordan's selection, along with Stephen Miller's appointment as the president's new chief of staff, highlights a shift towards a combative political approach, Sprunt says. Democratic leadership elections are expected to happen next week and are likely to keep current leaders Hakeem Jeffries in the House and Chuck Schumer in the Senate in place.

U.S. federal prosecutors have indicted three men accused of being Iran-backed operatives allegedly involved in nearly 20 terrorist attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the U.S. The charges include a plot in September against a British air base where American forces were stationed. The Justice Department says some of these attacks were directed live via FaceTime from Iraq.

  • 🎧 Federal prosecutors in Manhattan accuse the men of working for Iran's Revolutionary Guard and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah, both classified as terrorist groups, according to reporter Willem Marx. Seven of the attacks happened in Britain. They included arson, explosives and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London. Marx also noted that, in a separate case, British counter-terrorism police have arrested a 41-year-old U.S. Army soldier on suspicion of spying for Russia under the National Security Act. Authorities emphasized that this spying investigation is not linked to the Iran-related case. But Marx says these incidents raise significant concerns about security around American military bases in Britain and the safety of nearby residents.

Veterans in the new Congress

by Quil Lawrence, Veterans correspondent

A Navy admiral fired by the Trump administration is returning to Washington as a Democratic congresswoman. In Virginia, a former Army Colonel beat another former Army Colonel, and a female Navy vet won a rematch to unseat another female Navy vet. In Florida, a staunchly pro-Trump Air Force Vet narrowly fended off a former Army Brigadier General (both also women.) In Montana, two military veterans lost, splitting the votes against a Republican former attorney general with no military background.

What conclusion to draw? There isn't any!

Americans dependably say they admire military service, and political campaigns recruit vets to run on tough races. Whether it works remains an open question, though some research suggests Democrats in particular may benefit from veterans status with voters.

The next Congress includes at least 80 veterans, with a few races still too close to call. And according to With Honor, which supports veteran candidates from both parties who promise to sponsor legislation across the aisle, more than 50 vets in the next Congress have signed their pledge.

But the number of vets is shrinking, down to 15% from the 19% currently in office. That's probably just demographics. Relatively few Americans serve in today's all-volunteer military, while past generations were drafted by the millions to Vietnam and Korea. During World War 2, military service was almost a given for men. When that generation entered politics, both chambers had around 70% veterans for a decade, from 1965 to 1975.

The 120th Congress will host more female vets than ever, about double the last class. Analysis by the Veterans Campaign and the University of San Francisco found that Democrats chose veterans as candidates for the toughest races, in districts President Trump won in 2024 by an average of 22 points.

There's another way vets are serving: as poll workers. The group Vet the Vote recruits veterans and their families to help run elections. Starting from a goal of 150,000 volunteers during the 2024 presidential cycle, their campaign counted more than 175,000 for this midterm, from all 50 states, helping bolster the understaffed and overworked polling officials nationwide. The group says it had volunteers in 4 out of 5 zip codes across the country.

And veterans like to vote. Syracuse University D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families found that vets turned out in relatively higher numbers than civilians in every election since 2014, a difference especially pronounced in midterm elections.

Life advice

Being honest with people can be tricky. Sometimes, deciding whether to say anything at all can be harder than finding the right words to say. Social psychologist Vanessa Bohns says that giving feedback or criticism often feels like a dilemma. But with care, you can make better choices about when to share your thoughts. Bohns has shared three questions with Life Kit that you could consider before voicing your opinion.

  • 🗣️ Is this information helpful? Honesty is beneficial if your feedback helps someone improve, avoid embarrassment or learn something about themselves. If your comments are mean-spirited, irrelevant or impractical to enact, it's probably better to stay silent.
  • 🗣️ Would I want to hear this? Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the other person doesn't want to hear it. A 2022 survey found that people often underestimate others' desire for feedback even when it is constructive.
  • 🗣️ Do they want your feedback? When in doubt, don't assume you know what someone needs. Pre-assessing how valuable your advice is or how well someone can handle the truth can make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing.

For more guidance on how to share good and bad news, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

  • Volunteer musicians from Musicians On Call perform for veterans at the VA Medical Center in Washington, D.C., and other hospitalized patients nationwide. They typically visit hospitals three to four times a month.
  • The Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam came alive recently as a renowned tattoo artist brought 17th-century masterpieces to life on visitors' skin.
  • The Professional Women's Hockey League has announced the name of its new women's hockey team: the San José Sea Lions. (via KQED)

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: Iran-backed trio accused of plotting attacks on U.K. base hosting U.S. jets
entries.summary: Iran-backed operatives have been charged over nearly 20 attacks, including a plot on a U.K. base housing U.S. troops. Separately, a U.S. soldier is held in the U.K. on Russia spying claims.
entries.content:
Iran-backed trio accused of plotting attacks on U.K. base hosting U.S. jets

Federal prosecutors in New York have charged three men with terrorism offenses over what they describe as an Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The charges include a September plot against a British air base where American forces were stationed.

The indictment, unsealed on Tuesday, names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, 32, who holds Iranian and Iraqi citizenship, Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi.

Prosecutors allege the men acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah to orchestrate, plan and conduct the attacks through a network of associates across Europe and the U.S., targeting Jewish communities and a British base hosting American troops. The indictment cites plots against synagogues in London and in New York. Both Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hezbollah are designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organizations.

The court filings describe an operation that was directed, in part, by the suspects who were thousands of miles away. In April, prosecutors have alleged, the three men gathered in a room and watched an attack unfold live on a large screen via Apple's FaceTime video calling app. Al-Hassani allegedly coached the attacker through igniting and hurling a series of seemingly incendiary devices while Al-Saadi filmed.

The following day, Al-Hassani is accused of guiding another man on a video call as he lit an improvised explosive and threw it at a synagogue in London.

The men "helped orchestrate a campaign of terror" on behalf of the two designated terror groups, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald.

The RAF Fairford plot

The United Kingdom seems to have been a central target of the plot allegedly perpetrated by the three men: among the roughly 18 attacks claimed last spring by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, which prosecutors say was a front for Kata'ib Hezbollah, as many as seven took place in the U.K. It was the most intensely targeted country in Europe, though the indictment does not specify the location of other plots or attacks.

These included arson attacks, the use of explosives, and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London - one of whom was a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Prosecutors say that in April the men sat in a room, and directed an attack remotely, in real time, over FaceTime, telling the attacker when to light and throw what seems to have been some kind of incendiary device.

The next day, one of the men, Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, allegedly told another man attacking a London synagogue to "light it up like a Christmas tree."

According to the indictment, Al-Hassani was operating from Iran, but he began paying associates in Britain in August to film the perimeter of RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, several hours west of London.

They allegedly obtained vans and drums of fuel, looked into buying chemical accelerants, and gathered metal items that could potentially serve as shrapnel. The vans were fitted with sham branding for a fuel delivery firm as well as a pool supply company.

On September 26, three of these vans had set off toward the base that housed large numbers of U.S. military aircraft. At least two vehicles were stopped at a security roadblock, and British authorities seized all three early the next morning and arrested those inside.

The U.S. almost immediately redeployed several of its long range bombing aircraft from the base at the time of this incident.

The indictment said Al-Saadi had been detained abroad in May and brought to the United States, where prosecutors say he kept directing the network from his jail cell by relaying coded messages through phone calls with relatives in Iraq. He used aliases to refer to his alleged co-conspirators and referred to terrorist activity, including ongoing alleged plots, as "work," while those he spoke to used the phrase "international section" to mean overseas travel, according to the indictment. His sister and mother were among his interlocutors on some of those calls. Three days before the plot, in late September, he allegedly asked them to get money to Al-Hassani for the RAF Fairford operation.

British authorities had earlier charged two men with national security related offenses tied to the incident.

U.S. soldier held over Russia allegations

In a separate case, British counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday it arrested a 41-year-old member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain's National Security Act 2023. Officers have been searching two addresses in the same region of Gloucestershire, to the west of London. The man, who has not been named, has been held at a London police station. Police said the allegations concern Russia, and the investigation was "very much ongoing," according to Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK.

FBI Director Kash Patel called the arrest important in the context of an uptick in FBI counter-intelligence arrest, and said it "involves allegations of espionage" - without giving further details.

The man who's been held was a senior soldier, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command. His arrest was, he added, a "sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."

The U.S. footprint in Britain

Though unrelated, both these cases have occurred in the U.K., a country which hosts a large American military presence. At the start of the war in Iran, Britain's Ministry of Defence confirmed to the U.K. Parliament in March that U.S. forces operate eleven RAF bases across the country, with approximately 12,300 American military and civilian defense personnel at various sites.

Responding in January to a written question from a member of Parliament, the ministry said that there were around 11,000 uniformed U.S. personnel in the country, excluding families, civilians and contractors.

The ministry has declined to give figures for individual bases, citing the security of personnel.

The U.S. Air Force's two main operating bases are RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, in eastern England. Other sites include RAF Croughton, a communications station in Northamptonshire, and RAF Menwith Hill in North Yorkshire, used primarily by the National Security Agency, according to a House of Commons Library briefing. RAF Fairford serves as a forward operating base for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command.

In March, the British government allowed the U.S. to use British bases for limited strikes against missile sites in Iran, according to a parliamentary research service, which identifies Fairford as one of the bases potentially involved.

The threat picture around some U.S. bases seems to have sharpened in recent days. The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the U.S. military had moved aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall on Monday because of a threat from Iran. NPR did not independently confirm the reports.

Neither the U.K. nor the U.S. government has confirmed the reason for the aircraft movements that have been reported. Britain's Ministry of Defense has said aircraft relocate routinely for operational reasons.

entries.title: Both sides now? Critics slam DOJ moves to dismiss convictions of Trump allies
entries.summary: The DOJ moved to dismiss criminal convictions of former Trump adviser Steve Bannon and of the Oath Keepers, in what it calls "the interests of justice." Critics are crying foul.
entries.content:
Both sides now? Critics slam DOJ moves to dismiss convictions of Trump allies

The Biden-era Justice Department portrayed the contempt of Congress case against Steve Bannon as open and shut.

Bannon declined to cooperate with the House committee that investigated the siege on the U.S. Capitol, flouting a subpoena and refusing to show up for an interview. A trial jury in Washington, D.C., deliberated for less than three hours before delivering a guilty verdict. A federal appeals court upheld that verdict.

Now, four years later, the DOJ is asking a court to drop the case and erase the conviction "in the interests of justice." Bannon's lawyers do not oppose the move.

Legal experts said it follows a pattern where the Justice Department is helping to wipe the slate clean for allies of President Trump—with no one defending the cases, and without courts hearing arguments to the contrary. That violates the U.S. legal system's tradition of hearing views from opposing parties and comes as the Justice Department has also pursued investigations of Trump's perceived enemies.

"No adversity remains in this serious and high-profile criminal matter between, on the one hand, the U.S. Department of Justice overtly acting at the behest of the president of the United States, and on the other hand, Bannon, the defendant, who is a close political ally and adviser to the same president," said Bruce Searby, a defense attorney in Washington and a former federal prosecutor.

The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment about its decision to walk away from the conviction and the lack of adversity, or truly opposing parties, in the case. Bannon's lawyers did not return messages seeking comment.

Vacating convictions, issuing pardons

Searby first noticed the issue in April, when the DOJ asked to vacate the convictions of about a dozen leaders and deputies of the far-right Oath Keepers and Proud Boys groups.

Those seditious conspiracy trials took months to unfold, as juries heard details about how some of those extremists gathered weapons, recruited followers and even breached the Capitol in the worst attack since the War of 1812.

Trump pardoned the vast majority of Jan. 6, 2021, defendants on his first day back in office, calling them "patriots."

In a recent interview with the CBS newsmagazine 60 Minutes, Trump took credit for those pardons. "I don't think any group's been treated more unfairly than them, and to this day, when they see me they cry," he said.

The administration took another route in seeking to drop the cases of more senior members of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys—telling judges the move was in "the interests of justice." That was the same rationale it went on to use in the Bannon case.

Lawyers for Representative Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who served on the House Select Committee investigating the events of January 6, told a federal appeals court last spring this was not an ordinary set of cases—and that it should exercise its power to appoint a friend of the court, or amicus, to defend the convictions.

"The established path forward is for this Court to appoint an amicus to present opposing argument and defend the judgment being ambushed," wrote attorneys Justin Sher and Douglas Jensen.

Their court filing said judges have authority to take that step. And they pointed out two other controversial times that judges named outside lawyers to evaluate a bid to dismiss criminal charges: one in the case of former Trump national security adviser Michael Flynn; and another in the case of former New York City Mayor Eric Adams.

Ultimately, judges reluctantly dismissed the Jan. 6 charges without appointing a friend of the court.

"Today's epilogue diminishes the gravity of that day, denigrates the work of the prosecutors and law enforcement officers who secured these convictions, and excuses criminal acts that caused a centuries-long pillar of our democracy—the peaceful transfer of presidential power—to buckle," wrote U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta.

Leeway for prosecutors

Now, the issue has resurfaced in the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, who presided over Steve Bannon's trial in 2022.

In a court filing last week, DOJ said it would exercise its prosecutorial discretion to dismiss Bannon's indictment. Courts have recognized wide leeway for prosecutors in making decisions about their resources.

Deputy Associate Attorney General Michael Weisbuch wrote it was not appropriate to pursue the contempt case against Bannon because Bannon said he believed he was protected by executive privilege.

Weisbuch said the judge lacked authority to reject the unopposed motion to dismiss. "But even assuming any review could be proper, the policy-laden grounds for dismissal asserted above are not susceptible to judicial second-guessing," he added.

Searby, the former prosecutor, said the judge should not accept the DOJ argument "at face value" and dismissing the case should not be a "foregone conclusion."

An outside lawyer, he said, could assess whether the Justice Department's actions amount to an abuse of prosecutorial discretion: if they are taken in bad faith, tainted with impropriety or contrary to public interest.

Critics and good government groups said the Trump administration has been exploiting the legal system, which is designed to hear views from two opposing parties. The president famously sued his own government over the leak of his tax returns, and then negotiated a settlement with the Justice Department that handed him and his sons immunity from tax audits.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who previously served as a defense attorney for Trump, confronted serious questions about that deal and his sign-off during a confirmation battle in August. The Senate went on to approve his nomination by a single vote.

entries.title: Volunteer musicians play songs for veterans who are hospitalized
entries.summary: Volunteer musicians play for veterans and others who are hospitalized. They're part of Musicians On Call, a group that spreads the healing power of music.
entries.content:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Dante Ciolfi unzips his guitar case in a courtyard of the Veterans Medical Center in Washington, D.C.

"I'm about to tune my guitar," he says.

He is getting ready to play some songs for patients in the hospice wing of the hospital. Ciolfi is a musician volunteer with Musicians On Call or MOC, a non-profit that brings live music to hospital patients nationwide, both bedside and virtually via zoom. The group's motto is "delivering the healing power of music." When Ciolfi isn't volunteering, he teaches computer science to graduate students.

He meets up with Ellen Morris, another volunteer with MOC. She trains musician volunteers on hospital protocols and guides them from room to room.

Once they reach the hospital's hospice unit, Morris takes the lead and knocks on a patient's room door. "Hi there, how are you doing today? My name is Ellen with Musicians on Call," she says, "I have my friend Dante here that would love to play a song for you today, would that be OK?"

The patient, 93-year old Army veteran Lawrence Ludden, agrees. He is sitting in his room reading the newspaper, but he's quick to extend his hand to visitors.

Ciolfi thanks Ludden for the sacrifices he's made then he adjusts his guitar and begins singing, "Desperado," by the Eagles.

Ludden's room is filled with sunlight. His daughter Eillen Ludden is here on her daily visit.

He's the father of 4 and his shelf is full of family pictures — five grandchildren, two great-grandkids, a picture of him and his late wife on their wedding day and a couple of pictures of Ludden with England's Prince Harry who visited the VA this past August.

Once the song ends, and with a smile on his face, Ludden claps and thanks the volunteers. He also shares a memory with visitors.

"When I was a young boy I played piano, I used to like to sing quite a bit on the stage and I was in some light operas," Ludden says. "You never told me that," Morris replies.

Making the rounds while feeling gratitude for veterans

The volunteers move on to the next patient's room.

Ellen Morris says Ciolfi is an excellent volunteer. "The first time he played a song, and I watched him watch the reaction of the patient, it was overwhelming for me to see him be overwhelmed," Morris says. She knew right then that he was perfect for the group's mission.

Ciolfi says that playing music for veterans bedside is profound. He tries to hold emotional space with the patient, he says, even with those who can't speak.

"When I play, I try to mentally establish a conduit," says Ciolfi, "so the energy is kind of flowing back and forth. And to me that is so special … that energy is powerful."

That's clear when he plays for Marine veteran John Fay, who is in bed and non-verbal. Fay taps his heart with his hand as he listens to the music.

"To me that signals that he felt the music," says Nicolette Rubin, a music therapist in charge of the music program at the VA Medical Center in Washington, D.C.

"I think he was grateful, he wanted to kind of keep the beat and feel it in his body, and his soul. I think he felt it in his heart," Rubin says, adding that music is not only uplifting to the spirit, but it's a restorative treatment that helps patients recover from and cope with emotional and physical trauma.

Ciolfi says he's witnessed a multitude of reactions to his music in patients. "A woman all of a sudden broke into tears," he says, "and at first I was wondering what's going on. But then a smile came on her face and it was like, no need for words."

U.S. Airforce veteran Sidney Nichols whispers yes, when volunteer Morris asks if he wants to listen to music. He served as a pararescue specialist for four years in Southeast Asia, including in Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines.

Nichols is in bed, his eyes half-closed, but when Ciolfi starts singing "Crazy Love," by Van Morrison, he perks up and taps his hand on his leg as he silently begins mouthing the song's lyrics.

"You know that song, don't you? You were singing along," says Morris. Nichols responds, "I like it."

When asked how much Ciolfi knows about each patient's medical condition or their life, he's quick to respond. "I don't know anything about their circumstances," Ciolfi says. "Technically, I could probably read it on the chart that is outside their room. I intentionally don't because I want to stay focused on the music."

Musicians On Call volunteers have performed for more than a million patients across the country since the organization was founded in 1999. Musician volunteers typically go into hospitals 3 to 4 times a month.

"I appreciate the opportunity to do it. You know, to me it's a gift," Ciolfi says.

His immigrant parents came from Italy, he says early on they drilled into him how lucky he is to be a U.S. citizen.

"Every single day I'm experiencing freedoms that other countries have no concept of," Ciolfi says.

And those freedoms, he says, are protected by our veterans.

"If I can do one tiny thing like play a song, my gosh, I'm there."

Editor's note: Since reporting this story U.S. Airforce veteran Sidney Nichols has died.

entries.title: Oil giant ExxonMobil left Venezuela years ago. Now it's considering a return
entries.summary: ExxonMobil has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Venezuelan government and its state-owned oil company to explore opportunities in the country.
entries.content:
Oil giant ExxonMobil left Venezuela years ago. Now it's considering a return

ExxonMobil, the biggest U.S. oil company, is exploring a return to Venezuela after leaving almost two decades ago.

On Monday, the company announced it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Venezuelan government and its state-owned oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. The MOU, which is typically a non-binding agreement, involves ExxonMobil examining potential "upstream opportunities" – that refers to oil exploration and production.

ExxonMobil said in a statement, "We welcome the opportunity to evaluate potential upstream opportunities with the Venezuelan government and PDVSA."

A lot has happened in Venezuela's oil sector in the past ten months. In January, shortly after the Trump administration captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump gathered U.S. oil company executives in the White House and urged them to invest in the country. At that time, ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods said the country was "uninvestable."

But the country overhauled its petroleum law this year to make it more attractive for international oil companies. Those changes included allowing private oil companies more operational control in partnerships, as well as reforming taxes and royalties. The country has also welcomed the expansion of other U.S. oil companies, including Chevron and Continental Resources.

Still, ExxonMobil executives have maintained a cautious tone. On a call with analysts last month, Woods said that while there is "progress being made on those areas– working on fiscal regimes, working on legal regimes, working on investor protections, a number of things that are kind of in progress. But there's a way to go."

"This memorandum is a meaningful first step," ExxonMobil's statement reads, "But any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections and competitive returns."

ExxonMobil, which grew out of Standard Oil, operated in Venezuela for much of the 20th century. But over the years, the company's relationship with the Venezuelan government has been rocky. Beginning in 2004, then-President Hugo Chávez forcibly renegotiated contracts with international oil companies and ordered the nationalization of ExxonMobil assets. In 2007, ExxonMobil left the country.

Since then, ExxonMobil has been in international arbitration with the Venezuelan government. In September 2025, a U.S. court ordered Venezuela to pay ExxonMobil over $985 million for the past expropriations.

Energy analysts tell NPR that ExxonMobil may be looking at oil fields in Venezuela's Orinoco Belt, an area with sizable oil reserves and where the company has operated in the past.

The oil extraction process in this region generates a lot of greenhouse gas emissions, says Paasha Mahdavi, a political science professor at UC Santa Barbara who studies the oil industry.

Mahdavi says oil production in the Orinoco Belt has particularly high methane levels, a potent planet-heating gas. " This really matters from a global climate story," Mahdavi says.

ExxonMobil also has large oil investments in Venezuela's neighbor, Guyana, a key emerging player in the international oil industry. For years, Venezuela and Guyana have had a territorial dispute that has also been related to oil rights.

entries.title: U.S. officials look to Europe to learn how to make prison better
entries.summary: American prison officials are looking to European nations like Germany and Norway for a roadmap on how to design a prison that emphasizes rehabilitation and a successful return to life on the outside.
entries.content:
U.S. officials look to Europe to learn how to make prison better

More than a dozen New Yorkers crowded into an empty prison cell in Berlin, Germany, this October. Inside, they found many contrasts to U.S. prisons: For one, prisoners held at this German facility, Tegel Prison, have keys to their own cells.

The reason, prison director Martin Riemer told the group, is so the men held here can lock their own door when they go to work or school, just like someone might at home. The guards still have keys, but Riemer said this gesture offers a semblance of privacy.

Riemer also noted that every prison cell in Germany must have natural light and ventilation. In the cell the tour group inspected, the large window still had bars on it, but it opened. A breeze was blowing in.

The purpose of this trip was to inspire key players in the criminal justice system — a judge, a prosecutor, a prison official, among others — to see new ways of improving New York City's troubled jail system, which officials are in the process of reimagining.

The trip, organized by the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit, is part of a larger trend: U.S. officials are increasingly looking abroad for how to design a better prison or jail system. In fact, at least 10 U.S. states now model some of their prison units or practices after prison systems in Western Europe and Scandinavia.

"It's what happens when they get there that makes a world of difference, really seeing it with their own eyes," says Nancy La Vigne, dean of the Rutgers School of Criminal Justice. "Touring the facilities, talking to the officers, talking to the incarcerated population, witnessing rehabilitation in real time is very inspiring."

On the tour of Tegel Prison, the group from New York kept finding tangible differences. Jails and prisons in the U.S. often have a distinct smell — the result of many bodies held in a poorly ventilated space. This German prison did not. Jails and prisons in the U.S. are often noisy. This prison was quiet.

Aisha Elliott, a tour member who spent more than 20 years incarcerated in New York state prisons, noticed the furniture.

"There's a lot of wood and movable objects, which I think makes it more bearable. Everything in New York is steel, metal, thin and painful," said Elliott, chief program officer at the Women's Prison Association, an advocacy group.

Tina Luongo kept peeking at the cell toilets. In American jails, she says the toilets remind her of a metal dog bowl. In Berlin, most were porcelain, like in a home.

"It's speaking to me because it's the smallest thing," said Luongo, who leads the Legal Aid Society's criminal defense practice, the largest public defense provider in the U.S. "I have to believe that makes a difference in how you show up in those places."

The German prison system

European prisons aren't perfect. In countries like Norway and Denmark, prisons still experience overcrowding, understaffing and lockdowns. Officials at several German prisons were quick to tell the New York group that correctional officers often still have to deal with things like violence between prisoners and issues with drug overdoses.

German prisoners say that what they are experiencing is still prison: They long for more human touch, for instance, and better food.

But the country is often regarded as an international model. After the Holocaust, Germany adopted a new constitution that centers on protecting human dignity, including in its prisons. In Germany, the loss of freedom is seen as the punishment, not the conditions inside.

In contrast, prison conditions in the U.S. are often plagued with inhumane conditions and violence. The Department of Justice has dozens of open investigations into jails and prisons across the country for constitutional violations.

By law, life inside a German prison has to resemble life outside prison as much as possible, a concept known as normalization.

Lauren-Brooke Eisen, senior director of the Justice Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, says normalization might look like allowing prisoners to cook their own food, or wear street clothes instead of a uniform. It could also be that a toilet inside a cell has a door or curtain on it for privacy.

German prison staff also go through years of training, and many have backgrounds in social work or law. In the U.S., correctional officers often only train for a few weeks or months. All of this, Eisen says, creates a culture of rehabilitation in German prisons.

"In many other countries, when you are incarcerated, you don't lose your humanity the same way that you do necessarily in the United States," Eisen says.

European models in the U.S.

Over the last decade, the Vera Institute's own initiative, called Restoring Promise, has launched prison units modeled after Europe in six states: Connecticut, Massachusetts, South Carolina, North Dakota, Colorado and Idaho.

Its initiative focuses on 18- to 25-year-olds, a group that is more likely to make impulsive decisions, including resorting to violence to solve a conflict.

Ryan Shanahan, chief research officer at the Vera Institute, says prioritizing safety is necessary when any change happens inside a prison.

"But what does that mean? Traditionally in U.S. prisons, safety is keys, locks, cameras, barbed wire fences," says Shanahan, who helped start Vera's initiative.

But, Shanahan says, skills like asking questions, listening and relationship building can make an environment safer, too. The goal of the Vera Institute's prison units is to build that culture. Older prisoners serving long sentences act as mentors for young people in the program. Staff members engage with families on the outside.

There are daily schedules that include discussion groups and activities aimed at "learning conflict resolution and being able to practice it, learning to care for each other and be vulnerable and practice that, so that you can care and be vulnerable when you go home," Shanahan says.

That matters. Almost everyone who goes to prison in the U.S. is eventually released.

A cost-benefit analysis

But these types of programs are still in only a small percentage of U.S. prisons. One barrier to launching more of them is the sheer size of the U.S. prison system.

Around 2 million people are behind bars in the U.S. at any given moment, the most in the world. The German system is about 3% of that size. People in German prisons also generally serve sentences that are far shorter than those in the U.S.

Shanahan says for many U.S. prison leaders, the desire for change is there, but "there has to be a level of risk tolerance. There has to be a commitment to try to do something different."

Other key barriers include cost and staffing, says La Vigne, the Rutgers professor. Many U.S. prisons are currently facing staffing shortages.

"Most of the programs that have been piloted have a pretty high ratio of correctional officers to incarcerated persons," she says. "But investing those resources is probably cost beneficial because you'll also be retaining your officers and your staff, because they'll be more likely to feel like this is a place where I want to be."

There is evidence to suggest that both staff and prisoners benefit from programs like the German model.

In a 2023 study of one of its units in South Carolina, Vera found prisoners there were far less likely to commit violence, and also less likely to end up in solitary confinement.

In Washington, a program modeled after Norwegian prisons in partnership with the University of California, San Francisco, also resulted in less violence among prisoners, and correctional staff began coming to work more consistently.

When Maine remodeled its prisons around the concept of human dignity, it found prisoners were less likely to commit new crimes once they were released.

In Pennsylvania, a reform unit called Little Scandinavia saw almost no violent incidents in 2024, even as violence rose in other facilities, according to preliminary data cited in a Brennan Center report.

On its tour of Tegel Prison in Berlin, the New York group passed through a greenhouse that smelled like fresh dirt and lemon basil.

Inside, Lenny Albrecht, who has been incarcerated there for four years, was repotting plants. He said his job as a landscaper requires a lot of trust: He can use scissors and knives in his work, and he can walk the grounds without being supervised by an officer.

Mostly, though, he said he likes that the work makes him feel comfortable and relaxed.

"Before, I was very aggressive," Albrecht said. "The work here makes you calm down and relax. And that's a thing I never had before."

Nearby, Elliott, the women's prison advocate, is taking in the freshness of the place. The yards in New York prisons, she said, are mostly concrete.

"This feels good because they're treating people like people," she said. "I feel like they are headed in the right direction, which is toward release, supporting people toward their release."

She said a person in prison might not feel good about where they are, but the goal should be to make them feel good about who they are, or who they can become.

entries.title: Your guide to hosting a flavorful, cozy and stress-free Thanksgiving
entries.summary: Whether you're hosting friendsgiving or Thanksgiving, we've got foolproof turkey recipes, advice on how to stay present while hosting, and directions on how to create a stunning floral arrangement.
entries.content:
Every time I host Thanksgiving, it feels like a debate between what to repeat from last year and what to do differently this year.

Should I cook that turkey recipe again, or try a new one? Should I decorate the table with mini gourds again, or shake things up with a big sunflower centerpiece?

Let Life Kit help you decide. As you plan your Thanksgiving, friendsgiving or harvest-themed dinner party menu and decor, here are a few fresh ideas to add flavor, color and calm to the day. That includes two foolproof turkey recipes, advice on how to stay present while hosting, and directions on how to create a stunning floral arrangement with supermarket flowers.

Crowd-pleasing Thanksgiving recipes

Combine these recipes with sides and desserts — and you've got a whole feast. Don't forget to make Mama Stamberg's cranberry relish!

Easier roast turkey and gravy. Chef and writer Lan Lam shares the recipe she developed for America's Test Kitchen. It involves roasting the turkey on a pre-heated pizza stone to avoid the dreaded task of flipping the piping hot bird midway through the cooking process. It's the perfect recipe for first-timers. Get the recipe here. 

Salt-and-pepper roast turkey breast. Don't feel like fussing over a whole bird? Try a bone-in turkey breast. It's "significantly easier to cook, it takes a fraction of the time and it still feeds a group comfortably," says New York Times food writer Eric Kim. Get the recipe here.

Stuffing with a cheesy pizza twist. Kim's fun spin on traditional stuffing is sure to be a crowd pleaser. Day-old bread gets tossed and baked with tomato paste, oregano and mozzarella cheese. Get the recipe here.

Pane criminale, or pull-apart garlic bread. This is one of chef and writer Samin Nosrat's favorite things to bring to a group meal. In this recipe, the bread is sliced vertically instead of horizontally, guaranteeing that each slice of bread has garlic butter. Once you set it at the center of the table, "everyone just starts pulling it apart," she says. Get the recipe here.

Vegan mushroom-coconut vegetable pot pie. Don't leave your meatless friends behind. This pot pie recipe from Tracye McQuirter's book, Ageless Vegan, uses coconut milk and mushrooms to add heft and flavor. Be sure to use a vegan pie crust for the recipe. Get the recipe here.

Roasted vegetables with Korean-inspired magic sauce. This is chef and writer Roy Choi's version of his mom's magic sauce. It uses Korean ingredients like gochugaru and gochujang, and tastes terrific spooned over roasted vegetables. Get the recipe here.

Make hosting fun, easy — and less stressful

Host with "generous authority." When it comes to the event itself, a host should absolutely be able to enjoy themselves, but that doesn't mean stepping back entirely, says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering.

The most meaningful gatherings tend to be run by what Parker calls "generous authority." She defines this as "imposing in a way that serves your guests."

It's about finding a balance between encouraging new connections and letting them happen naturally. "When you give guardrails, people then [are] allowed to actually be incredibly spontaneous because they feel safe." 3 ingredients for hosting with "generous authority." 

Ask your guests "magical questions" to spark engaging conversations. It's "a question everyone in your group is interested in answering" and hearing the answers to, says Parker. For example: What's the weirdest thing you've ever found in your pocket? What topic could you give a 20-minute talk on with no preparation?

She likes asking them in group settings because they have the power to cut through small talk and reveal people's personalities. And people don't need to agree or have the same tastes or experiences to answer. Parker shares a few favorite magical questions here.

Pick three moments you want to be present for. You probably won't have the time and attention for everything on your to-do list, so shorten it down to the moments that matter to you most, says Niro Feliciano, a psychotherapist and author of All is Calmish: How to Feel Less Frantic and More Festive During the Holidays.

Maybe that's decorating the Thanksgiving table, serving homemade roasted turkey, and watching the football game. In those moments, show up as much as you can. How to focus on what matters during the holidays.

Decorating tips to make your house feel cozy and festive

Put holiday decor in the first spot people see when they enter your house. "Designers never leave that empty because the eye has to have somewhere to land, and it needs to land on something very pretty," says Elaine Griffin, interior designer and author of Design Rules: The Insider's Guide to Becoming Your Own Decorator.

So place a centerpiece in that spot, she says. It can create the same effect as filling a room up with holiday knickknacks. You can make a centerpiece by thrifting a glass vase and filling it with, say, pinecones or cranberries.

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste.

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom and displaying decorative gourds. More holiday decorating tips here.

Arrange supermarket flowers like a pro. Florist Alexander Campbell of AC Floral Studio explains how to make a professional-looking floral arrangement for your tablescape using store-bought flowers.

First, look for one to two types of greenery with different textures and three to four types of flowers in your color palette. Then, to build your bouquet, add each item in this order. See the infographic below for examples.

  • Start with greenery.
  • Then add filler flowers.
  • Next, add tall flowers to create a high point.
  • Then add "star" flowers that really speak to you.
  • Finish off your arrangement with dainty flowers.

See a step-by-step guide on how to make an arrangement here.

This story includes reporting and writing from Marielle Segarra, Andee Tagle, Beck Harlan, Margaret Cirino, Lennon Sherburne, Audrey Nguyen, Lauren Migaki, Meghan Keane, Maria Godoy, Clare Marie Schneider, Diba Mohtasham and Sam Yellowhorse Kesler. It was edited by Clare Marie Schneider. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.

entries.title: AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect
entries.summary: Swatters are increasingly using AI technology that creates synthetic voices or sound effects to generate remarkably believable fake emergency calls to law enforcement.
entries.content:
In August, a caller made a bomb threat to Wheatland Union High School in Yuba County, Calif.

Police responded overnight and classes were canceled. There was no bomb and no one was hurt.

Authorities said it was part of a series of hoax calls — also called swatting — made to schools across the country over the summer.

Swatting calls can be made to 911 or police departments, with callers reporting a bomb threat, mass shooting or some other kind of life-threatening emergency with the intention of initiating a massive emergency response, according to the FBI.

911 dispatchers have long dealt with this problem. But the incident in Yuba County was different: The call was made by an AI-generated voice, a new and growing challenge for emergency responders.

"Those voices [of swatting callers] used to be pretty easy to recognize, but now they're natural sounding. They can insert pauses. They can use words like, 'uh', or 'maybe, um, let me think about it.' And it sounds very natural," says Mel Maier, the CEO and executive director of APCO International, the Association of Public Safety Communication Officials.

The goal of swatting calls is to harass or retaliate against the targets of the calls — like a public official. They usually trigger a big, chaotic response from police, redirecting public safety resources from real emergencies.

People also have been killed and injured in swatting attacks, Maier notes.

Swatting calls made by people using AI-generated voices or background sounds are making these hoax calls sound even more realistic, and harder to determine what's real and what isn't.

APCO and NENA: The 9-1-1 Association, which both represent 911 dispatchers, say incidents like the one in Yuba County reflect their growing worries over how AI could be used by bad actors.

APCO and the Public Safety Threat Alliance, an information-sharing and cybersecurity group, looked into the prevalence of swatting to 911 call centers. They published their findings in June based on 766 responses from public safety communications professionals. About 14% of dispatchers said they were targeted using AI tools. Maier says he thinks that number is going to keep going up with increasingly advanced tools

Signs of a swatting call

Companies like ElevenLabs, an artificial intelligence company creating synthetic voice software, offer AI tools that are incredibly cheap and readily available, according to Brandon May, an assistant professor of forensic psychology at the Florida Institute of Technology.

"I'm able to clone my voice on ElevenLabs for less than $20, and I can change the intonations. I can change how deep or high-pitch my voice is. I can change the pauses," he says.

And this makes it hard for anyone to detect these AI fakes.

"It is no longer simple to just look at an image or hear a video or hear a voice and go, 'That is AI.' People are duped by this all the time," he says.

Elaborate fraud callers using AI chatbots are even tricking people into handing over their life savings, May says.

And the increasing sophistication of these fake voices and sound effects makes it especially difficult for emergency dispatchers to deduce what is real or not during what May calls "high-stakes, high-consequence" calls. "It is going to be nearly impossible to detect," he says.

Despite the difficulty, APCO and NENA are developing ways to train their members to deal with these new threats.

April Heinze, NENA's vice president and chief of 911 operations, says there are some hallmarks of a swatting call.

For example, most swatters do not dial 911 directly.

"The reason being is 911 provides location. It provides a callback number. It provides the name of the person who owns the phone. It provides a lot of extra data, and it's really impossible to spoof your location on 911," she says.

Swatting calls are usually made to police departments or courthouses, Heinze explains. These callers are then ultimately transferred into the 911 centers. So trying to trace those calls is impossible, she says.

Training evolves to address new AI threat

Both Heinze and Maier decline to describe the specifics of training to identify potential AI swatting calls. The more information available, they say, the easier it will be to train AI to fool dispatchers going forward.

Maier does note one idea for training. APCO is working to create training criteria on caller interrogations where the dispatcher asks the caller specific questions at "such granular level that an AI cannot scoop that information from a public database, cannot capture it from a social media post, or simply make guesses," he says.

Despite the growing concerns about the use of AI, both Maier and Heinze emphasize that dispatchers will always assume calls reporting a life-threatening situation are real — and will continue sending emergency resources to any call for help.

"It's important to understand that no matter what, public safety is going to have a very strong response," Heinze says. "Even if there are indicators that it is a swatting incident. They are always reporting a life-or-death situation, and if it's a life-or-death situation, you cannot ever take chances on that."
